title: AI labs want in-house auditors — but maybe they should shut the front door first
slides: AI labs hire internal auditors, but who watches the watchers?
They fear regulators might miss hidden dangers in models.
Yet most risks come from open-source weights and insider access.
So the real fix is locking down training data and compute.
Close the front door before hiring more auditors.
thread_text:
1. Who Audits AI?

AI labs now hire internal auditors to check their models. But those auditors report to the same people building the systems. That's a conflict, not oversight.

2. Oversight Theater

Internal audit teams often lack access to training data or compute logs. They review polished reports, not raw model behavior. Regulators might inherit the same blind spots.

3. Open Weights, Real Risk

Most dangerous capabilities leak through open-source releases and insider access, not closed APIs. Auditors chase the wrong door. The threat walks in through the side.

4. Lock Data and Chips

If you control training runs and hardware, you control capability. Auditing outputs after release is too late. Compute and data are the real chokepoints.

5. Check Your Own Stack

Ask your AI vendor: who can access training data and compute? If they can't answer, you're exposed. Do that before trusting any audit report.

instagram.caption:
AI labs are hiring internal auditors who report to the same people building the models. That's not oversight, that's a mirror. 🪞

They worry regulators will miss hidden dangers, yet most risky capabilities leak through open-source weights and insider access, not closed systems.

The real fix isn't more auditors. It's locking down training data and compute before anything ships. 🔒

If you publish AI-generated content, ask your vendor who can access their training runs. If they can't answer, your work is exposed. ⚠️

So who actually audits the auditors you're trusting? 🤔
